metaDescription: Six gooseneck tablet stands compared, from clamp-on bed mounts to heavy floor bases, for hands-free reading and viewing from any position.
introParagraphs: A gooseneck stand bends where you want it and stays there, which makes it the most forgiving design for a tablet over a bed, chair or counter. There are no knobs to loosen and no presets to pick, just a flexible arm that you shape by hand. The six stands here use that idea in three ways: heavy floor bases, a floor tripod and clamp-on mounts.

The spread in reach and mounting is wide. The Macally clamp has an 11 inch neck and handles devices up to 8 inches, the LanPavilion has a 15.7 inch gooseneck on a 1.8 kg base, and the VIVI MAO runs 30 inches for bed clamping. At the top end the Lamicall floor stand raises its arm to 63 inches on a 10.6 lb base, and the Weilisi tripod extends from 13.5 to 82 inches.

We evaluated each pick based on product specs and buyer feedback, weighing stability, arm length, device range and the way each stand attaches. The best gooseneck depends on where it mounts, so we separate floor, tripod and clamp picks in the sections below. Pay attention to device weight limits, because a long flexible arm can sag under a heavy tablet.

products.name: Lamicall Gooseneck Tablet Floor Stand
products.description:
The Lamicall is the gooseneck floor stand to buy when you want the least wobble. It carries a heavy 10.6 lb base that keeps the arm from pulling the stand over, and the arm and extension pole are premium solid aluminum alloy. Height adjusts from 130 cm (51.2 inches) to 160 cm (63 inches), so it reaches a person lying in bed or sitting upright.

The flexible arm bends easily to the position you want, and the universal ball on the back of the clamp lets you rotate the tablet. Its minimum height is also relatively tall, so it is aimed at bed and recliner use rather than low tables.

Setup is a matter of assembling the pole and arm, and care means wiping the metal. Compared with the LanPavilion it is much heavier and taller, and compared with the Weilisi it is more stable but less adjustable in range. For a permanent bedside setup it is the most confident choice.
products.bestFor: A permanent bedside or recliner setup with maximum stability
pros: Solid aluminum alloy arm and pole
cons: Too heavy to move around daily

products.name: LanPavilion Gooseneck Tablet Floor Stand
products.description:
The LanPavilion balances reach and size better than most floor stands. It has a 15.7 inch gooseneck that bends by hand, mounted on a wide, heavy base that weighs 1.8 kg. It holds phones and tablets between 4.7 and 13 inches, which includes most iPads and Galaxy Tabs.

The weight is lower than the Lamicall's, so a heavy tablet in a thick case will lean on the arm. It is better for lighter loads, such as an iPad Air or a smaller tablet. The wide base compensates for the lighter weight by spreading the footprint.

Setup is quick and cleaning is a wipe. Against the Lucky Trip it uses a similar floor-and-gooseneck layout, but its 1.8 kg base is a clear published number, which makes it easier to judge. It suits a nightstand or a kitchen counter better than a recliner with a long reach.
products.bestFor: A moderate-reach gooseneck on a nightstand or counter
cons: Short arm for a deep recliner

products.name: VIVI MAO Gooseneck Clamp Tablet Mount
products.description:
The arm is about 30 inches long, made of a heavy-duty aluminum-magnesium alloy with a stiffened cord. A reinforced, thickened clamp base grips the headboard or table edge with non-slip silicone pads.

A clamp needs something sturdy to grab, so a flimsy headboard or a very thick edge will not work. Because there is no floor base, there is no footprint on the carpet, which is a real convenience in a small bedroom. The long 30 inch arm also flexes more than a short one, so expect some bounce when you tap the screen.

Assembly is a matter of tightening the clamp, and cleaning is a wipe. Compared with the Macally it carries larger devices up to 12.9 inches and reaches farther. If your bed frame has a sturdy edge, it is a low-cost way to float a tablet.
products.bestFor: Clamping a tablet to a headboard or bedside table at the lowest cost
pros: 30 inch arm reaches over the bed
cons: Needs a sturdy edge to clamp to

products.name: Lucky Trip Floor Stand with Double Weight Base
products.description:
The Lucky Trip is a floor stand with a 13.7 inch gooseneck and a double weight base. It rotates 360 degrees, so you can flip between portrait and landscape. The listing says it can sit on the floor or on a desk, which gives it some versatility.

The double weight base is described but its weight in pounds is not stated in the listing we have, so you cannot rank its stability numerically. The gooseneck is a bit shorter than the LanPavilion's, so reach is limited. Cases wider than 4.3 to 9.8 inches will not fit the clamp, which is a concrete fit check.

Setup is quick and care is a wipe. If you want a weighted floor gooseneck without paying for the Lamicall, it is a reasonable middle option.
products.bestFor: A lower-cost weighted gooseneck for floor or desk use
pros: Works on a desk or the floor
cons: Base weight is not stated in pounds
Cases must fit a 4.3 to 9.8 inch clamp width

products.name: Weilisi Heavy-Duty Tripod Stand with Gooseneck
products.description:
The Weilisi is a tripod with a gooseneck, and its 13.5 to 82 inch height range is the widest here. It has a dual clip configuration with silicone protection pads on both the phone clip and the tablet clip. An included remote helps with video calls or recording.

Because it is a tripod, the legs spread across the floor, so you need clear space. At full 82 inch height the whole stand wobbles more, so use lower settings when you can. The gooseneck lets you angle the screen after the height is set.

Setup involves extending the legs and tightening the locks. Compared with the Lamicall it offers a larger height range and a remote but a lighter base feel. It suits someone who stands, sits and lies down in different spots and wants one stand to do it all.
products.bestFor: One tall stand shared between standing, seated and reclined use

products.name: Macally Adjustable Gooseneck Phone and Tablet Clip

specList.label: Fit
specList.value: Includes 9.7 inch iPad and iPad Pro 10.5

products.description:
The Macally is the compact pick: an 11 inch gooseneck with a clamp that grips tables, desks and counters up to 1.75 inches thick. It works with phones and tablets whose display width is under 8 inches, including the 9.7 inch iPad and iPad Pro 10.5 according to the listing. It clips and removes easily, so it moves between rooms.

The device limits are the main drawback. A larger tablet is outside the stated range, and an 11 inch neck is short for a bed. It is a counter and desk stand more than a bedside stand.

There is nothing to assemble, and cleaning is a wipe. Against the VIVI MAO it has a shorter reach and smaller device range, but it moves around more easily. It is best for a phone or small tablet in a kitchen or at a workbench.
products.bestFor: A small tablet or phone clipped to a counter or desk
pros: Clamps surfaces up to 1.75 inches thick
cons: Limited to devices under 8 inches wide
Neck is short for bed use

buyingCriteria.explanation: Gooseneck stands attach three ways. The Lamicall, LanPavilion and Lucky Trip stand on a floor base, the Weilisi uses tripod legs, and the VIVI MAO and Macally clamp. A clamp needs a sturdy edge, with the Macally limited to surfaces up to 1.75 inches thick. Choose by the furniture you have, not by arm length alone.

A long flexible arm acts like a lever, so base weight decides tipping. The Lamicall uses a 10.6 lb base, the LanPavilion a 1.8 kg base, and the Lucky Trip a double weight base. Research on floor stands puts roughly 4.5 lb as a minimum base for a full size iPad at full extension. Heavier tablets and thick cases may need more.

Arm lengths run from 11 inches on the Macally to 30 inches on the VIVI MAO. A longer arm reaches farther but bounces and droops more under load. Choose the shortest arm that reaches your eyes. Check that the arm holds your tablet's weight without sagging.

The Macally handles devices under 8 inches wide, the VIVI MAO covers 4.7 to 12.9 inches, and the Lamicall, LanPavilion and Lucky Trip cover up to 13 inches. Cases add weight at the end of the arm. Weigh the tablet with its case and compare with the listing. A device near the limit will make the arm droop sooner.

The Weilisi runs from 13.5 to 82 inches, the Lamicall from 51.2 to 63 inches, and the clamp stands depend on where you mount them. A screen held low pushes the neck forward, so raising it toward eye level helps. Pick a range that matches your seated or reclined eye line. Choose the lowest height that still keeps the screen comfortable.

The Lucky Trip lists a clamp width of 4.3 to 9.8 inches, and the Weilisi uses silicone protection pads on both clips. A wide clamp holds a case better. Check the width of your tablet with its case before you buy. Tablets with bulky cases are the most likely to slip in a narrow clamp.

howWeEvaluated.title: Stability
howWeEvaluated.description: The Lamicall's 10.6 lb base and the LanPavilion's 1.8 kg base lead among floor stands, while clamps like the VIVI MAO depend on the surface. This is based on specs and buyer feedback, not hands-on measurement.

howWeEvaluated.title: Arm quality
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at arm length and material. The VIVI MAO uses a heavy-duty aluminum-magnesium alloy at 30 inches, and the Lamicall uses solid aluminum alloy. A longer arm earns credit only if it resists droop.

howWeEvaluated.title: Reach and height
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the height ranges, from the Weilisi's 13.5 to 82 inches to the Macally's compact 11 inch neck. Reach matters for beds and recliners, while short necks work for counters. Stands that reach farther but wobble were not rewarded for range alone.

howWeEvaluated.title: Device compatibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked supported sizes and clamp widths. The Macally is limited to devices under 8 inches wide, while the Lamicall and LanPavilion reach 13 inches. We also noted case fit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed price tier against reach and stability without quoting figures. The VIVI MAO is the lowest-cost pick, and the Lamicall is the highest.

cards.label: Floor base
cards.text: The Lamicall, LanPavilion and Lucky Trip stand on their own weight. They need no sturdy furniture but take floor space. Choose one if your headboard is flimsy or you want to move the stand.

cards.label: Clamp
cards.text: The VIVI MAO and Macally clamp to an edge. They save floor space and cost less but need a solid surface. The Macally handles surfaces up to 1.75 inches thick.

cards.label: Our recommendation
cards.text: Pick the VIVI MAO if your bed has a sturdy edge, and the Lamicall if you want the most stable setup.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for a stable mount and an arm that reaches your eyes without bouncing. A heavy base or a clamp on a solid frame beats a light stand.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Lamicall reaches 63 inches on a 10.6 lb base, while the VIVI MAO clamps a 30 inch arm to the headboard. Choose between them based on whether you prefer a floor or a clamp.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if you use a large tablet daily in bed. The Lamicall's 10.6 lb base is the main reason.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if you have a sturdy headboard or only use a phone. The VIVI MAO and Macally cover that at lower tiers.

faq.q: How do I choose between a floor gooseneck and a clamp?
faq.a: Choose by your furniture. A floor stand like the Lamicall needs no sturdy edge but takes floor space. A clamp like the VIVI MAO saves space but needs a solid headboard or table edge. If your bed frame is thin or flimsy, a floor stand is safer.

faq.q: How much do gooseneck tablet stands cost?
faq.a: The range runs from the VIVI MAO at the lowest tier to the Lamicall at the highest. The extra cost buys base weight and metal quality. For casual use, a clamp or lighter floor stand is enough, and daily bed use justifies a heavy base.

A long flexible arm bends under the weight of the device and case. Shorter arms sag less, and heavier tablets sag more. Choose the shortest arm that reaches your eyes, and check the listing's device weight limit.

faq.q: Can a gooseneck stand hold a large iPad?
faq.a: Several can. The Lamicall, LanPavilion and Lucky Trip list support up to 13 inches. Research suggests a base around 4.5 lb for a full size iPad at full extension, so a heavier base is wiser. Thick cases add weight and may need a heavier option.

faq.q: Will the clamp damage my furniture?
faq.a: The VIVI MAO uses non-slip silicone pads and the Weilisi uses silicone protection pads on its clips. Pads reduce marks but do not eliminate them on delicate finishes. Use a thin cloth if you are worried. Check that the surface thickness is within the clamp limit.

faq.q: Can I use a gooseneck stand for video calls?
faq.a: Yes, if you can raise the camera near eye level. The Weilisi reaches 82 inches and includes a remote. A low tablet shows chins and ceilings. Test the angle before a long call.

faq.q: How do I care for the stand?
faq.a: Wipe the metal and pads with a dry cloth and tighten clamps occasionally. Do not bend the arm back and forth repeatedly, as that can fatigue the metal. A stable surface and gentle handling keep it working for years.
